html:
The Tokugawa shogunate was the military government of Japan from 1603 to 1868, ruling from Edo, now Tokyo. The map shows it in 1650, 1700 and 1715; the chart's bar is Tokugawa Japan.

Tokugawa Ieyasu won the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600, ending more than a century of civil war, and became shogun in 1603. The emperor stayed in Kyoto with no real power. Some 250 to 300 lords, the daimyō, ran their own domains but had to spend every other year at Edo, which kept them loyal and drained their money.

The shogunate banned Christianity and, under the policy later called sakoku, closed Japan to most foreigners. Only the Dutch and Chinese could trade, at Nagasaki, the Dutch on the island of Dejima. Japan had peace for over two centuries. Edo grew past a million people, farming output rose, and merchants paid for a lively city culture of kabuki theater and woodblock prints.

In 1853 American warships under Perry forced the country open. The shogunate lost authority, and in 1868 the Meiji Restoration handed power back to the emperor.
